claim: The endothelial blood-brain barrier (BBB) strictly controls immune cell trafficking into the central nervous system (CNS).
source: The endothelial blood-brain barrier (BBB) strictly controls immune cell trafficking into the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive literature and is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In neuroinflammatory diseases such as multiple sclerosis, the tight control of immune cell trafficking by the BBB is disturbed, leading to immune cell infiltration into the CNS.
source: In neuroinflammatory diseases such as multiple sclerosis, this tight control is, however, disturbed, leading to immune cell infiltration into the CNS.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about multiple sclerosis pathology.

claim: UFMTrack achieves 90% track reconstruction efficiency.
source: UFMTrack achieves 90% track reconstruction efficiency and allows for scaling due to the reduction of the analysis cost and by eliminating experimenter bias.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: UFMTrack eliminates experimenter bias.
source: UFMTrack achieves 90% track reconstruction efficiency and allows for scaling due to the reduction of the analysis cost and by eliminating experimenter bias.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data between manual and automated analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Immune cell extravasation across the vascular wall is a multistep process regulated by the sequential interaction of different signaling and adhesion molecules on the endothelium and the immune cells.
source: Immune cell extravasation across the vascular wall is a multistep process regulated by the sequential interaction of different signaling and adhesion molecules on the endothelium and the immune cells (Nishihara et al., 2020; Marchetti and Engelhardt, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The multistep extravasation process includes tethering and rolling to reduce travel speed, shear-resistant arrest, polarization, and crawling of the immune cell on the luminal surface of the endothelium, and finally immune cell diapedesis across the endothelial layer.
source: These molecular interactions mediate distinct sequential steps, namely tethering and rolling to reduce travel speed, shear-resistant arrest, polarization, and crawling of the immune cell on the luminal surface of the endothelium and, finally, immune cell diapedesis across the endothelial layer (Marchetti and Engelhardt, 2020; Nourshargh and Alon, 2014; Nourshargh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on immune cell extravasation.

claim: The precise molecular mechanisms mediating the multistep immune cell extravasation in each organ depend on the immune cell subset and the specific characteristics of the vascular bed.
source: The precise molecular mechanisms mediating the multistep immune cell extravasation in each organ depend not only on the immune cell subset but also on the specific characteristics of the vascular bed.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The BBB establishes a tight barrier that strictly controls the transport of molecules across the BBB, ensuring tissue homeostasis required for neuronal function.
source: For example, in the central nervous system (CNS), the endothelial blood-brain barrier (BBB) establishes a tight barrier that strictly controls the transport of molecules across the BBB, ensuring tissue homeostasis required for neuronal function (Marchetti and Engelhardt, 2020; Engelhardt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T cells crawl for very long distances against the direction of blood flow on the surface of the BBB endothelium in search of permissive locations for diapedesis.
source: For instance, T cells crawl for very long distances against the direction of blood flow on the surface of the BBB endothelium in search of permissive locations for diapedesis (Bartholomäus et al., 2009; Lyck and Engelhardt, 2012; Castro Dias et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Research on T-cell interaction with the BBB has been successfully translated into therapies in the clinic.
source: Research on T-cell interaction with the BBB has already been successfully translated into therapies in the clinic (Steinman and Zamvil, 2005; Singer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Upon arrest, T cells polarize and either crawl at speeds between 3 and 10 µm/min over the brain endothelial monolayer or probe the endothelial monolayer by remaining rather stationary and sending cellular protrusions into the endothelial monolayer.
source: These studies have shown that upon their arrest, T cells polarize and either crawl at speeds between 3 and 10 µm/min over the brain endothelial monolayer or probe the endothelial monolayer by remaining rather stationary and sending cellular protrusions into the endothelial monolayer (Figure 1D; Steiner et al., 2010; Rudolph et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Both crawling and probing behaviors can lead to diapedesis of T cells across the brain endothelial monolayers.
source: Both behaviors can lead to diapedesis of the T cells across the brain endothelial monolayers.
evidence: This is inferred from the description of T cell behaviors and their outcomes.

claim: The diapedesis process lasts at least 3–5 min, with some immune cells observed to protrude and retract several times prior to finalizing a prolonged diapedesis process to the abluminal side of the brain endothelial monolayer.
source: This process lasts at least 3–5 min, with some immune cells observed to protrude and retract several times prior to finalizing a prolonged diapedesis process to the abluminal side of the brain endothelial monolayer (Castro Dias et al., 2021; Abadier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: T cells that have successfully migrated across the brain endothelial monolayer usually continue to migrate underneath the endothelial monolayer.
source: Finally, T cells that have successfully migrated across the brain endothelial monolayer usually continue to migrate underneath the endothelial monolayer (Shulman et al., 2009; Arts et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Manual analysis of in vitro flow assays is time-consuming and requires offline frame-by-frame analysis of imaging data.
source: The data analysis of these 'in vitro flow assays' requires time-consuming offline frame-by-frame analysis of the imaging data by individual experimenters, in which the dynamic interactions of each individual immune cell has to be followed over the entire time of the assay manually and assigned to specific categories.
evidence: This describes the current state of manual analysis methods.

claim: Manual analysis is prone to inevitable errors and subjective judgments.
source: Thus, this manual analysis is prone to inevitable errors and subjective judgments of the various experiments.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of manual analysis.

claim: The time-consuming manual T-cell tracking limits the number of events that can be studied and thus the statistical power of the analysis.
source: Furthermore, the time-consuming manual T-cell tracking limits the number of events that can be studied and, thus, the statistical power of the analysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of time-consuming manual analysis.

claim: Automation of the analysis is hampered by the use of unlabeled cells imaged by phase contrast, which poses a challenge due to the similar grayscales and morphology of immune cells and brain endothelial cells.
source: It is, however, hampered as these assays are usually performed with unlabeled cells and imaged by phase contrast (Figure 1C), which poses a challenge due to the similar grayscales and morphology of the immune cells interacting with the brain endothelial cells.
evidence: This describes technical challenges in developing automated analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: T cells instantly appear within the field of view when perfused on top of endothelial cells in the presence of shear flow.
source: When perfused on top of the endothelial cells in the presence of shear flow, at first T cells instantly appear within the field of view (FoV).
evidence: This describes an observed phenomenon in the experimental setup.

claim: T cells are often either suddenly displaced over a certain distance or completely detached and washed away during the assay.
source: Later on they are often either suddenly displaced over a certain distance or completely detached and washed away (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes observed T cell behavior illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The 2D+T model outperformed the 2D model by 9% according to the average precision (AP) metric for T-cell mask prediction.
source: In the T-cell mask prediction task, the 2D+T model outperformed the 2D model by a notable 9% according to the average precision (AP) metric (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: For the transmigration mask, the 2D model performance reached only 54%.
source: At the same time, for the transmigration mask, which is much more difficult to infer, the 2D model performance reached only 54%, which is insufficient for reliable detection of T cells migrating across the pMBMEC monolayer.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model evaluation.

claim: The 2D+T model outperformed the 2D model by 32% AP for transmigration mask prediction.
source: In this task, the 2D+T model outperformed the 2D model by 32% AP.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model comparison.

claim: The 2D+T model was sensitive to frame misalignment, leading to false positive detection of transmigrated T cells.
source: We observed that the 2D+T model was sensitive to frame misalignment, leading to false positive detection of transmigrated T cells.
evidence: This is an observation from model testing.

claim: After increasing to physiological flow rates, a significant number of T cells detached from the pMBMEC monolayers, with higher numbers of T cells detaching from non-stimulated pMBMEC monolayers when compared to those stimulated with pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: After increasing to physiological flow rates (Steiner et al., 2010), a significant number of T cells detached from the pMBMEC monolayers, with higher numbers of T cells detaching from non-stimulated pMBMEC monolayers when compared to those stimulated with pro-inflammatory cytokines as detected by the distribution of the track ending times between 5 and 30 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the CD4+ T-cell analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The data obtained with UFMTrack were in accordance with previous observations obtained by manual frame-by-frame analysis.
source: The data obtained with UFMTrack were in accordance with our previous observations obtained by manual frame-by-frame analysis (Steiner et al., 2010; Abadier et al., 2015; Haghayegh Jahromi et al., 2019).
evidence: This validates the automated method by comparison with previous manual analysis cited in the literature.

claim: Statistically significant differences in the mean T-cell motility parameters were observed depending on the pMBMECs stimulation condition.
source: As shown in Figure 4C–H, we observed statistically significant differences in the mean T-cell motility parameters depending on the pMBMECs stimulation condition.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: Differences in the shape of the distribution of T-cell crawling speeds were observed, consistent with previous reports of underlying differences in the mechanisms mediating T-cell crawling on non-stimulated vs cytokine-stimulated pMBMECs.
source: Furthermore, we observed differences in the shape of the distribution of T-cell crawling speeds, consistent with our previous reports of underlying differences in the mechanisms mediating T-cell crawling on non-stimulated vs cytokine-stimulated pMBMECs (Haghayegh Jahromi et al., 2019).
evidence: This finding is consistent with previous research cited.

claim: An increased variance of the T-cell instantaneous speed on stimulated compared to non-stimulated pMBMECs was observed.
source: While not statistically significant for the IL1-b and with a low significance for the TNF stimulations, an increased variance of the T-cell instantaneous speed on stimulated compared to non-stimulated pMBMECs is observed (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increased variance of T-cell instantaneous speed suggests that T-cell crawling is often interrupted by T-cell recognizing specific cues on the stimulated endothelium.
source: This suggests that T-cell crawling is often interrupted by T-cell recognizing specific cues on the stimulated endothelium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: The T-cell meandering index distribution was high on non-stimulated and lower on stimulated pMBMECs.
source: The T-cell meandering index distribution was high on non-stimulated and lower on stimulated pMBMECs (Figure 4H), underscoring that cytokine stimulation enhances directed T-cell movement on the pMBMEC monolayer.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Cytokine stimulation enhances directed T-cell movement on the pMBMEC monolayer.
source: The T-cell meandering index distribution was high on non-stimulated and lower on stimulated pMBMECs (Figure 4H), underscoring that cytokine stimulation enhances directed T-cell movement on the pMBMEC monolayer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the meandering index data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The average speed experienced during accelerated movement is significantly lower for the IL1-b condition.
source: This detachment kinetics is reflected in the average speed experienced during accelerated movement, which is significantly lower for the IL1-b condition (Figure 4I), suggesting the need to break more bonds with the endothelium when pro-inflammatory cytokines are present.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The lower accelerated movement speed for IL1-b condition suggests the need to break more bonds with the endothelium when pro-inflammatory cytokines are present.
source: This detachment kinetics is reflected in the average speed experienced during accelerated movement, which is significantly lower for the IL1-b condition (Figure 4I), suggesting the need to break more bonds with the endothelium when pro-inflammatory cytokines are present.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the accelerated movement data.

claim: Cytokine stimulation of pMBMECs, although applied from the luminal side, also affected T-cell movement at the abluminal side of the pMBMEC monolayer.
source: Interestingly, cytokine stimulation of pMBMECs, although applied from the luminal side, also affected T-cell movement at the abluminal side of the pMBMEC monolayer.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of transmigrated T cells shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The results obtained by the automated analysis were in full agreement with the manual analysis performed by the experienced experimenter.
source: The results obtained by the automated analysis were in full agreement with the manual analysis performed by the experienced experimenter.
evidence: This is a comparison result shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The data highlight the variability of the results from the inexperienced experimenters, confirming the potential for significant experimenter bias.
source: At the same time, the data highlight the variability of the results from the inexperienced experimenters, confirming the potential for significant experimenter bias.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing results of different experimenters shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: T-cell detection efficiency by UFMTrack was above 90%.
source: By this approach, we found T-cell detection efficiency to be above 90% (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The appropriate T-cell density for automated analysis of their migration behavior on pMBMEC monolayers is 200–300 cells per FoV of the size of 3.8 mm2 or 50–80 cells/mm2.
source: These findings set the appropriate T-cell density for automated analysis of their migration behavior on pMBMEC monolayers to 200–300 cells per FoV of the size of 3.8 mm2 or 50–80 cells/mm2.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the detection efficiency findings.

claim: UFMTrack achieves a comparable T-cell tracking efficiency when compared to the manual analysis.
source: In Figure 5E, we show that our pipeline achieves a comparable T-cell tracking efficiency when compared to the manual analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison shown in Figure 5E.

claim: UFMTrack performs better than less experienced experimenters in T-cell tracking.
source: While its performance was not superior to that of the experimenter with 4 years of expertise in the analysis of the under-flow datasets, it does perform better than less experienced experimenters.
evidence: This is a finding from the tracking efficiency comparison.

claim: Data obtained for the CD8+ T-cell migration speed on pMBMECs was comparable between all experimenters and the automated analysis.
source: Data obtained for the CD8+ T-cell migration speed on pMBMECs was comparable between all experimenters and the automated analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Results obtained for the T-cell crawling speed were significantly different between the automated approach and manual analysis.
source: In contrast, results obtained for the T-cell crawling speed were significantly different between the automated approach and manual analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Manual analysis contains significant errors in the assignment of the T-cell position, leading to a jittery pattern in the T-cell migration tracks and overestimating the T-cell path and crawling speed.
source: Taking a closer look at the T-cell tracks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we readily observed that the manual analysis contains significant errors in the assignment of the T-cell position. This leads to a jittery pattern in the T-cell migration tracks and overestimates the T-cell path and, thus, T-cell crawling speed.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of tracks shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The experienced experimenter outperforms the inexperienced experimenters by a factor of 3 in analysis time.
source: Clearly, the experienced experimenter outperforms the inexperienced experimenters by a factor of 3.
evidence: This is a finding from time tracking data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: A researcher would spend 8.1 hr analyzing a dataset with 300 T cells when only the tracks of crawling T cells (50%, i.e. 150 cells) are analyzed.
source: On average, a researcher would thus spend 8.1 hr analyzing a dataset with 300T cells when only the tracks of crawling T cells (50%, i.e. 150 cells) are analyzed.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the time tracking data.

claim: If all T-cell tracks were to be analyzed manually, the analysis time would increase to 12.9 hr.
source: If all T-cell tracks were to be analyzed, this time would further increase to 12.9 hr.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the time tracking data.

claim: The UFMTrack framework reduces analysis time by a factor of 3 when analyzing only crawling cells and 5 if all cell tracks are to be analyzed.
source: The UFMTrack framework reduces analysis time by a factor of 3 when analyzing only crawling cells and 5 if all cell tracks are to be analyzed (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is a finding from time comparison shown in Figure 5K.

claim: With an average analysis time of 2.3 hr, the 10 experiments carried out in 1 day can be thoroughly analyzed within 1 day of machine time.
source: With an average analysis time of 2.3 hr, the 10 experiments carried out in 1 day can be thoroughly analyzed within 1 day of machine time.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the automated analysis time.

claim: The segmentation and transmigration detection quality for hPBMCs on HBMEC was sufficient to perform cell migration analysis.
source: While the endothelial cells look significantly different than the pMBMECs, the segmentation and transmigration detection quality was sufficient to perform the cell migration analysis.
evidence: This is confirmed by visual inspection mentioned in the text and data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Despite the different behavior and appearance of macrophages compared to T cells, the segmentation quality was sufficient to perform cell tracking and analyze cell motility parameters.
source: Despite the different behavior and appearance of the macrophages as compared to the T cells, the segmentation quality was sufficient to perform the cell tracking and analyze cell motility parameters (Figure 6E and F), as confirmed by visual inspection of the macrophages masks and cell tracking results (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is confirmed by visual inspection and data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Due to the different appearance of the flattening crawling cells and the transmigrated cells, the transmigration detection trained on the mouse T cells does not perform sufficiently well for the robust detection of transmigrating macrophages.
source: Nonetheless, due to the different appearance of the flattening crawling cells and the transmigrated cells, the transmigration detection trained on the mouse T cells does not perform sufficiently well for the robust detection of transmigrating macrophages.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the model for macrophages.

claim: Despite human T cells and EECM-BMECs being of different species, the T cells were successfully segmented, and their transmigration was detected.
source: Despite the cells being of different species, the T cells were successfully segmented, and their transmigration was detected, as confirmed by visual inspection of the T-cell and transmigration masks and cell tracking results (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is confirmed by visual inspection and data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Differences in migration statistics, migration and crawling speed of crawling T cells, and relative displacement of T cells treated with blocking antibodies versus control condition were confirmed.
source: We have confirmed the differences in migration statistics (Figure 6J and K), migration and crawling speed of the crawling T cells (Figure 6H), as well as the previously reported difference in relative (normalized to track path length) displacement (Figure 6I) of the T cells treated with anti-α4-integrin+anti-β2-integrin blocking antibodies (bab) and control (ctrl) condition (Soldati et al., 2023).
evidence: This confirms previous findings cited and is shown in Figure 6H-K.

claim: In the absence of ICAM-1, T cells were moving in the direction of flow.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Steiner et al., 2010; Soldati et al., 2023) where the analysis was performed using the ImageJ (Rueden et al., 2017) either manually or with the TrackMate (Ershov et al., 2022) plugin, we observed that in the absence of ICAM-1, T cells were moving in the direction of flow (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is consistent with previous observations cited and shown in Figure 6N.

claim: UFMTrack allows for capturing the rapid accelerated motions of the cells and thus reconstructing longer continuous T cell tracks.
source: At the same time, UFMTrack allows for capturing the rapid accelerated motions of the cells and thus reconstructing longer continuous T cell tracks.
evidence: This is a capability of the UFMTrack framework demonstrated in the analysis.

claim: UFMTrack enables capturing the migration properties of the consecutive steps of the T-cell migration cascade on the cell-by-cell basis.
source: This enables capturing the migrations properties of the consecutive steps of the T-cell migration cascade on the cell-by-cell basis.
evidence: This is a capability of the UFMTrack framework.

claim: The existing particle and cell tracking toolkits consider migration of one cell type and thus are not suitable for the detection of distinct migration regimes and cell interactions.
source: The existing particle and cell tracking toolkits consider migration of one cell type and thus are not suitable for the detection of distinct migration regimes and cell interactions (Allan et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2019; Ershov et al., 2022; Ulicna et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of existing tools supported by citations.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, none of the existing algorithms consider migration under the flow causing rapid cell displacement.
source: Furthermore, to our knowledge, none of the existing algorithms consider migration under the flow causing rapid cell displacement.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the approach based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: By establishing the detection of T-cell crawling, probing, transmigration, and accelerated movement combined with reliable T-cell tracking, UFMTrack enables in-depth analysis of distinct migration regimes on a cell-by-cell basis.
source: By establishing the detection of T-cell crawling, probing, transmigration, and accelerated movement combined with reliable T-cell tracking, we have enabled the in-depth analysis of distinct migration regimes on a cell-by-cell basis.
evidence: This summarizes the capabilities enabled by UFMTrack.

claim: UFMTrack allows for performing a thorough analysis of 10 experiments that a researcher can carry out in 1 day within 1 day of machine time.
source: We have demonstrated that the automated analysis performs on par with manual analysis while improving accuracy and eliminating experimenter bias, and enables scalability of flow-based immune cell migration experiments by reducing the analysis cost and lifting the burden of time-consuming manual analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the practical benefits of UFMTrack based on the time analysis data.

claim: The automated analysis performed with UFMTrack improves accuracy compared to manual analysis.
source: We have demonstrated that the automated analysis performs on par with manual analysis while improving accuracy and eliminating experimenter bias, and enables scalability of flow-based immune cell migration experiments by reducing the analysis cost and lifting the burden of time-consuming manual analysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of crawling speed measurements showing errors in manual tracking.

claim: One current limitation of UFMTrack is the performance reduction when the density of migrating T cells significantly increases (>250 cells/dataset).
source: One current limitation of the method is the performance reduction of the T-cell tracking when the density of migrating T cells significantly increases (>250 cells/dataset).
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method.

claim: The recommended T-cell concentration for UFMTrack analysis is about 100–150 k/ml.
source: Thus, the recommended T-cell concentration is about 100–150 k/ml.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the performance characteristics.

claim: Currently, UFMTrack does not consider dividing immune cells.
source: Another limitation is that currently, we do not consider dividing immune cells.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current implementation.

claim: Cell division events happen rarely (<1% of T cells) in the study of immune cell interaction with the BBB model.
source: While cell division events happen rarely (<1% of T cells) and are not primary events for the study of immune cell interaction with the BBB model, the modular architecture of our framework will facilitate future extension to detect cell division.
evidence: This is an observation about the frequency of cell division in these experiments.

claim: UFMTrack contributes to the 3R principle by reducing the number of animals to be sacrificed.
source: By enabling experiment scalability, unbiased analysis with advanced accuracy, and an in-depth analysis of large datasets of T-cell dynamics under flow, the computational and analytical framework presented here contributes to the 3R principle when studying the interaction of cells derived from animal models by reducing the number of animals to be sacrificed.
evidence: This is a claim about the ethical benefits of the method based on its improved efficiency.

claim: UFMTrack can be employed for fundamental research of the molecular mechanisms governing immune cell trafficking across a range of vascular beds.
source: UFMTrack can be employed for fundamental research of the molecular mechanisms governing immune cell trafficking across a range of vascular beds, screening of pharmaceutical treatments, as well as for personalized medicine based on the evaluation of treatment efficacy on patient-derived T-cell migration behavior on patient-derived endothelial monolayers.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of UFMTrack.

claim: UFMTrack can be used for screening of pharmaceutical treatments.
source: UFMTrack can be employed for fundamental research of the molecular mechanisms governing immune cell trafficking across a range of vascular beds, screening of pharmaceutical treatments, as well as for personalized medicine based on the evaluation of treatment efficacy on patient-derived T-cell migration behavior on patient-derived endothelial monolayers.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of UFMTrack.

claim: UFMTrack can be used for personalized medicine based on the evaluation of treatment efficacy on patient-derived T-cell migration behavior on patient-derived endothelial monolayers.
source: UFMTrack can be employed for fundamental research of the molecular mechanisms governing immune cell trafficking across a range of vascular beds, screening of pharmaceutical treatments, as well as for personalized medicine based on the evaluation of treatment efficacy on patient-derived T-cell migration behavior on patient-derived endothelial monolayers.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of UFMTrack.

claim: UFMTrack can be suitable to study cancer cell metastasis across different endothelial cell monolayers.
source: One can furthermore envisage that UFMTrack can be suitable to study cancer cell metastasis across different endothelial cell monolayers.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of UFMTrack.

claim: The developed framework can be extended to real-time operation during image acquisition.
source: Eventually, the developed framework can be extended to real-time operation during image acquisition.
evidence: This is a speculation about future development of UFMTrack.

claim: pMBMECs were isolated from 8- to 12-week-old C57BL/6J WT mice.
source: pMBMECs were isolated from 8- to 12-week-old C57BL/6J WT mice and cultured exactly as described before (Steiner et al., 2010; Coisne et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Intact pMBMEC monolayers were stimulated with 10 ng/mL of recombinant mouse TNF, 20 ng/mL of recombinant mouse IL1-β, or 5 ng/mL recombinant mouse TNF+100 U/mL recombinant mouse IFN-γ 16–24 hr prior to the assays.
source: Intact monolayers were stimulated or not with 10 ng/mL of recombinant mouse TNF, 20 ng/mL of recombinant mouse IL1-β, or 5 ng/mL recombinant mouse TNF+100 U/mL recombinant mouse IFN-γ 16–24 hr prior to the assays as previously described (Haghayegh Jahromi et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: During the accumulation phase, T cells at a concentration between 55 and 166 k/mL were perfused on top for 5 min under low shear stress of 0.1 dynes/cm2.
source: During the accumulation phase, T cells at a concentration between 55 and 166 k/mL were perfused on top for 5 min under low shear stress of 0.1 dynes/cm2, allowing them to settle on top of the pMBMEC monolayer.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: After the accumulation phase, the flow was increased to physiological levels with a flow shear stress of 1.5 dynes/cm2 to study postarrest T-cell behavior on pMBMECs for 27 min.
source: Afterward, the flow was increased to physiological levels with a flow shear stress of 1.5 dynes/cm2 to study postarrest T-cell behavior on pMBMECs for 27 min (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol illustrated in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The time-lapse imaging was performed using phase-contrast imaging at a frame rate of 6 or 12 frames/min, subsampled to 6 frames/min and resolution of 0.629 µm/pixel with a ×10 objective.
source: The time-lapse imaging was performed during both accumulation and physiological flow phases using phase-contrast imaging at a frame rate of 6 or 12 frames/min, subsampled to 6 frames/min and resolution of 0.629 µm/pixel with a ×10 objective.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used.

claim: The data was acquired in tiles of 870×650 µm2 (1389×1041 pixels) with an overlap of 100 µm, leading to a total acquired image area of 3170×1220 µm2.
source: The data was acquired in tiles of 870×650 µm2 (1389×1041 pixels) with an overlap of 100 µm, leading to a total acquired image area of 3170×1220 µm2.
evidence: This describes the imaging acquisition parameters.

claim: For each experiment, the dataset consists of 30 time frames of T-cell accumulation and 162 time frames of dynamic T-cell interactions with the pMBMEC monolayer under physiological flow.
source: For each experiment, the dataset consists of 30 time frames of T-cell accumulation and 162 time frames of dynamic T-cell interactions with the pMBMEC monolayer under physiological flow.
evidence: This describes the dataset structure.

claim: The segmentation models were implemented in TensorFlow.
source: The models were implemented in TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the implementation framework used.

claim: The training was performed on a dataset corresponding to 154 Megapixels of raw image data.
source: The training was performed on a dataset corresponding to 154 Megapixels of raw image data using the annotation mask for T cells ('T-cell mask') and the mask of the transmigrated part of the T cells ('transmigration mask'), the centroids map, and the weight map (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the training dataset size.

claim: For validation, 37 Megapixels of raw imaging data were used.
source: For validation, 37 Megapixels of raw imaging data were used.
evidence: This describes the validation dataset size.

claim: The 2D model has approximately 3 M parameters.
source: The models have approximately 3 and 8 M parameters correspondingly, and the model architectures are summarized in Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: The 2D+T model has approximately 8 M parameters.
source: The models have approximately 3 and 8 M parameters correspondingly, and the model architectures are summarized in Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: The framework was able to successfully detect cells of sizes that differ by almost a factor of two.
source: The framework was able to successfully detect the cells of sizes that differ by almost a factor of two (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: By discriminating cells by size, it is possible to extend UFMTrack to study the interaction of several types of immune cells migrating on top of a cellular monolayer under flow and imaged by phase contrast.
source: This demonstrates that, simply by discriminating cells by size, it is possible to extend UFMTrack to study the interaction of several types of immune cells migrating on top of a cellular monolayer under flow and imaged by phase contrast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells of different sizes can be detected.
